howTheStimulusArose: STATED PLAINLY BECAUSE IT DIFFERS FROM THE PLAN'S PRESCRIPTION.
M2b prescribes a provenance-bound disposable fork as the stimulus, and its stated reason is
that no lint-failing commit can otherwise reach a branch the canary watches: `push.branches` is
exactly [main, alpha], both are protected by ruleset Control with an empty bypass_actors, and
no additional in-repo branch can match.
The M2a catch-up merge falsified that assumption. Merging main into alpha (PR #86, 92 commits)
carried a PRE-EXISTING SC2250 in .githooks/pre-commit that is `new` relative to alpha's older
baseline but baseline relative to main. The commit reached alpha legitimately, through the PR
process and its five required checks, and the canary then fired on the push.
The outcome was PREDICTED BEFORE THE MERGE, not rationalised after: the same single SC2250 was
identified on PR #86's advisory trunk-check run and reported to the maintainer, who elected to
accept it rather than fix it first. So the diagnostic was known in advance and then observed.
WHAT THIS DOES NOT ESTABLISH: it is not a fork-based stimulus, and it was incidental rather
than deliberately induced. A reviewer who reads M2b's prescription as normative rather than as
one means to the end should treat M2b's runtime half as still open and run the fork exercise.
The argument for accepting it: the requirement is to CAUSE a controlled canary failure and
record the tuple bound to a lint diagnostic, and this observation is on production
infrastructure rather than a fork — the path that actually matters.
whatRemainsForM2b: If the fork-based stimulus is judged necessary, it still needs: a provenance-bound disposable
fork whose default branch is named `main`, carrying the same canary workflow at the same SHA
pins, with GitHub Actions ENABLED in that fork (they are disabled on forks by default, and
without enabling them the stimulus silently produces nothing and this half is unfalsifiable).
whyItLivesHere: It was first written to a standalone `COREDEV-2780-m2b-canary.json`, which the contract has
never heard of and nothing reads. §7's inventory and its ownership table both already assign
this observation to THIS file: `cell 16's ruleset read and its canary runtime control`, and
`the control proving the Trunk step stays observably failed while the job stays non-blocking`.
The repo has paid for that shape once already — `_recorded_remote_halves()`'s docstring
records rollout.json being named as owner in prose and parsed by nothing (codex, PR #84).
Conforming the evidence to the contract is cheaper and truer than amending the contract to
match where the evidence happened to land.

cell12DualBaseCheckRuns.what: §7 row 12's dual-base provenance-bound check runs, and the strict/advisory discrimination they carry.
why: A GREEN run cannot prove the gate is strict. With no findings, advisory and strict both
conclude success — they are indistinguishable. Only a RED run discriminates:
advisory  Trunk fails -> job failure -> WORKFLOW RUN SUCCEEDS
strict    Trunk fails -> job failure -> WORKFLOW RUN FAILS
That is why M3 requires both per base, and why revision 1 of the plan was wrong to accept a
context observed only while failures were suppressed — one that had never been able to fail.
A check run describes the JOB, so `checkRunConclusion` cannot by itself name which step
failed. M3's checklist binds the TRUNK STEP's API-reported `conclusion`, so each half below
records it as `trunkStepConclusion`, read from the workflow-jobs record.
stepScope.jobIdIsCheckRunId: That endpoint returns the job id, and on both runs below it equals the `checkRunId` already recorded (101560257395, 101560280950), so the step record is addressable from what is here with no second identifier to drift.

note: Meaningful as STRICT green only because the red observation below establishes that this
workflow version has no continue-on-error. PR #92 is branched from #91, so both ran the
same strict workflow via the pull_request merge ref.

boundDiagnostic.why: A setup, checkout or network failure would also fail the run while Trunk never reached lint evaluation. This names the linter, file, line and column, so the failure is bound to lint rather than to infrastructure.

note: THE WORKFLOW RUN CONCLUSION IS WHAT DISCRIMINATES STRICT FROM ADVISORY. Under M2's advisory
exemption this would read `success` with the job still `failure`. It reads `failure`, so the
job-scoped continue-on-error is genuinely gone.
The step conclusion is a SEPARATE requirement, not that inference: `trunk` (step 6) is the only
step that failed — steps 1-5, set-up, checkout and the three guards, all concluded `success` —
so the failure is located at lint evaluation, not upstream of it.
The PR is never merged, BY INSTRUCTION. Pre-M4 that is DISCIPLINE, not enforcement:
`trunk-check` is not one of Control's five required contexts (rollout.json records
`trunkCheckAbsentPreM4: true`), on de88d32 all five required contexts are `success` with only
`trunk-check` `failure`, and GitHub therefore reports PR #92 `mergeable: MERGEABLE`,
`mergeStateStatus: UNSTABLE` — its name for `mergeable, with a non-required check failing`.
Control's empty bypass_actors guarantees only that those five cannot be WAIVED; it cannot make
a non-rule block a merge. Its other rules, `deletion` and `non_fast_forward`, do not stop a
fast-forward push either, so no ruleset route is closed on this SHA (derived from the rules; no
push was attempted). What holds this commit off `main` is the never-merge instruction plus the
local pre-commit gate recorded below — which is itself bypassable. M4 makes this enforcement.

howTheRedCommitWasMade: The local pre-commit trunk gate BLOCKED the lint-failing commit, correctly — stopping new
findings is its purpose. Producing red-run evidence therefore requires --no-verify, which is
inherent to the observation rather than a shortcut, and is recorded here so it is not mistaken
for carelessness. The checks --no-verify skips were run by hand first: gitleaks on the staged
change (no leaks), version-sync, plugin assembly, hooks manifest.

cell2RetargetObservation.what: §7 cell 2's RETARGET case: the `edited` activity type fires on a base change, and the range `trunk check` receives is re-resolved against the NEW base.
why: `.github/workflows/trunk-check.yml` carries `types: [opened, synchronize, reopened, edited]`.
`edited` is the activity type a RETARGET fires; without it a retargeted PR keeps a green check
computed against the OLD base. That widening was a STATIC clause assertion — cell 2 records that
'nothing yet observes that it works'. This key is that observation, made for the first time.
`main` and `alpha` differ in exactly ONE file, docs/planning/evidence/COREDEV-2780-rollout.json,
and main's copy is strictly newer (alpha's is an ancestor version). That asymmetry decides
whether the experiment can discriminate at all, so the direction was MEASURED with
`git merge-tree --write-tree` against the real SHAs before the PR was opened, not reasoned about.
measured: cut from main,  retargeted main -> alpha : range 1 file -> 2 files   DISCRIMINATES
cut from alpha, retargeted alpha -> main : range 1 file -> 1 file    DOES NOT
directionIsLoadBearing.whyTheOtherDirectionFails: Cutting from alpha, the merge against main resolves rollout.json to main's newer copy, so the range is identical before and after. The observation would then look the same whether the range was re-resolved or carried over — an observation consistent with two worlds, which is the shape this project has repeatedly recorded as the benign one.

cell2RetargetObservation.theDiscriminator: docs/planning/evidence/COREDEV-2780-rollout.json can appear in the resolved range ONLY if the upstream was `alpha`: relative to `main` that file is unchanged, so it cannot enter diff(main_tip, merge). The changed-file list therefore IDENTIFIES the base directly rather than inferring it from run timestamps.
cell2RetargetObservation.howTheRangeIsObserved: The `guard-empty-diff` step prints the resolved range to stderr as `  changed: <path>` lines. Retrieved with `gh run view <runId> --log`. The upstream SHA itself is not echoed by that step, so the file list is the observable, which is why the fixture was designed to make the file list differ.
theResult: FOUR runs exist on the one head SHA fd60453, and they partition EXACTLY at the retarget:
before 17:00:16 — two runs, range 1 file,  computed against main
after  17:00:16 — two runs, range 2 files, computed against alpha
All four are recorded above rather than the two that make the cleanest pair, because a selective
record of a four-run population is not evidence. The new run appeared 4 SECONDS after the base
change, so `edited` fired; and its range contains rollout.json, so it was resolved against alpha.
The head SHA never changed, which is the whole point: the same commit, ranged against two bases.

theDiscrimination: Same file. Same base. Same PR. The two pre-existing MD038 findings at 2692 and 3018 stayed
SUPPRESSED IN BOTH RUNS — `2 existing issues` appears in the green half and in the red half alike.
What changed is one newly-introduced MD040 at 3046, and that alone moved the run from success to

failure. The gate scopes to something FINER THAN THE CHANGED FILE — the file was checked, its two pre-existing findings were seen, and only the new one failed the run. Whether that finer unit is the FINDING'S NOVELTY or merely the TOUCHED LINE is NOT settled by this evidence; see `aTHIRDWORLDTHISCANNOTSEPARATE` immediately below. The previous revision concluded `newly introduced findings, not changed files`, which asserts the novelty reading the adjacent key says is unproven (codex, PR #101).

why: The two held findings (MD038) sit at lines 2692 and 3018, which this PR does not touch. The
reported finding (MD040) sits at 3046, which it does. So two mechanisms produce IDENTICAL evidence:
(i)  the gate holds findings that are not NEW            <- what the cell claims
(ii) the gate holds findings on lines that did not CHANGE <- indistinguishable here
The recorded observation does not separate them, and the fixture as built never could: both edits
are appends at EOF, so every pre-existing finding is necessarily on an untouched line.
aTHIRDWORLDTHISCANNOTSEPARATE.whatWouldSeparateThem: A third commit that MODIFIES a line already carrying a pre-existing finding without introducing a new one. Under (i) it stays green; under (ii) it goes red. Not performed.
aTHIRDWORLDTHISCANNOTSEPARATE.statedRatherThanImplied: Recorded because the cell's wording ('passes for its pre-existing findings') reads as claim (i), and an unqualified record would let a later reader take (i) as observed when only the conjunction of (i)-or-(ii) is.

doesNotEstablish: Neither half says anything about a REQUIRED context; that is M4.
Cell 3(b) is observed for markdownlint on a Markdown file. It is not a claim that every linter in the
configured set scopes to new findings the same way — and the rejected validate-hooks.py candidate is
on any modified file regardless of whether the finding pre-existed. That asymmetry is a real property
of the gate, discovered here, and it is NOT covered by cell 3(b) as written.
The backlog figure is a measured lower bound over five files, not a re-derivation of 9027.
It does not separate per-ISSUE novelty from per-touched-LINE scoping — see `cell3b.aTHIRDWORLDTHISCANNOTSEPARATE`. Both produce identical evidence on this fixture.
Cell 3(a)'s cleanliness is positive-controlled for SHELLCHECK ONLY, not for every linter applicable to a .sh file — see `cell3a.thePositiveControlLIFTSONLYSHELLCHECK`.

It does not establish cell 3's NAMED PROPERTY ('the gate does not over-reach'). For the configured formatters that property is observed to be FALSE -- see `theGateDOESOverReach` and COREDEV-2850. This key records instances (a) and (b) for LINT findings only.

theGateDOESOverReach.severity: COUNTEREXAMPLE to cell 3's stated property. Not a scope note.
theGateDOESOverReach.theProperty: Cell 3 is titled 'The gate does not over-reach'. (a) and (b) are INSTANCES of that property, not a definition of it.
theCounterexample: Under `--upstream`, the two families of finding are scoped DIFFERENTLY:
linters    (shellcheck, markdownlint, ruff, mypy) -- pre-existing findings on a touched file
are reported as `N existing issues` and SUPPRESSED. Correct.
formatters (isort, black, prettier) -- evaluated WHOLE-FILE and reported as NEW on any
modified file, whether or not the file was already unformatted.
So an otherwise clean edit to an already-misformatted file FAILS THE GATE FOR DEBT IT DID NOT
INTRODUCE. That is the behaviour cell 3 exists to forbid.
